intro: What happens between typing a web address and seeing a page, plus the codes and terms engineers use to talk about it.

1.summary: Clients, servers, URLs, HTTPS and DNS.

lesson.title: Clients and servers: a restaurant
lesson.body:
Picture a restaurant.

- You, the diner, are the **client**: your browser or phone app.
- The kitchen is the **server**: a computer somewhere that's always on, waiting for orders.
- The waiter carrying your order there and your food back is **HTTP**, the set of rules for requests and responses.

You send a **request** ("give me the homepage"), and the server sends a **response** (the page, or an error). Every page, image and API call works this way.
lesson.pm: When something is slow, the first question is "client or server?" Is the phone slow to draw the page, or is the kitchen slow to cook?

lesson.title: Reading a URL
lesson.body:
A **URL** is a web address. Take it apart:

```
https://shop.example.com/products/shoes?color=red
```

- `https://` is the protocol. The **S** means secure, so the connection is encrypted.
- `shop.example.com` is the **domain**, which names the server.
- `/products/shoes` is the **path**: which page or resource.
- `?color=red` is the **query string**: extra details, like filters.

**DNS** is the internet's phone book. It turns `example.com` into the numeric address (an **IP address**) of the actual server.
lesson.pm: Query strings often carry tracking and filter state. That's why you should never put personal data in them: URLs get logged and shared.

cards.back: The device or app making a request, like your browser or phone app.
An always-on computer that receives requests and sends back responses.
The rules for web requests and responses. HTTPS is the encrypted, secure version.
A web address: protocol + domain + path (+ optional query string).
The internet's phone book: turns domain names into server IP addresses.
The part of a URL after `?`, carrying extra details like `?color=red`.

quiz.q: In the restaurant analogy, what is the server?
quiz.why: The kitchen fulfils orders (requests). The diner is the client; the waiter is HTTP.
Everything after `?` is the query string.

options: Turns domain names into IP addresses
Encrypts traffic between you and a site
Stores the files that make up a site
Speeds up pages by caching them nearby
quiz.why: DNS is the internet's phone book. Encryption is HTTPS; caching nearby is a CDN.

quiz.q: What does the S in HTTPS add?
quiz.why: HTTPS encrypts traffic so others can't read it.
The path says which page or resource on that server.

2.summary: Status codes, GET vs POST, localhost, ports, CDNs and latency.

lesson.title: Status codes and methods
lesson.body:
Every response comes with a three-digit **status code**:

- **2xx = success**: `200 OK`, `201 Created`
- **3xx = go elsewhere**: `301 Moved Permanently`
- **4xx = the request's fault**: `400 Bad Request`, `401 Unauthorized` (who are you?), `403 Forbidden` (I know you, but no), `404 Not Found`, `429 Too Many Requests`
- **5xx = the server's fault**: `500 Internal Server Error`, `503 Service Unavailable`

Requests also have a **method**, the verb. **GET** fetches something, and **POST** sends or creates something. You'll also see PUT/PATCH (update) and DELETE.
lesson.pm: 4xx vs 5xx is a quick triage tool: 4xx usually means the client sent something wrong; 5xx means the back end broke and needs attention.

lesson.title: localhost, ports, CDNs and latency
lesson.body:
**localhost** means "this very computer." When Claude Code starts a **dev server** (a test version of your app), it runs on your laptop at an address like `http://localhost:3000`.

The `3000` is a **port**, a numbered door on the computer. One machine can run many services, each behind its own door.

A **CDN** (content delivery network) keeps copies of files on servers around the world, so users get them from somewhere nearby, fast.

**Latency** is the delay before a response starts arriving. It's measured in milliseconds (ms).
lesson.pm: "It works on localhost" means it works on the engineer's laptop, not necessarily for real users. It's a milestone, not a launch.

cards.back: The three-digit result of a web request, e.g. 200 OK or 404 Not Found.
4xx = problem with the request (client side). 5xx = the server broke.
401 = not logged in or unknown. 403 = known, but not allowed.
GET fetches data. POST sends or creates data.
"This computer": used for running and testing apps on your own machine.
A numbered door on a computer (like `:3000`) that lets one machine run many services.
Content delivery network: copies of files on servers worldwide for faster loading.

quiz.q: Your logs show lots of `503` errors. Where is the problem most likely?
quiz.why: 5xx codes mean the server failed. 503 = service unavailable.

quiz.q: Which status code means "logged in, but not allowed"?
quiz.why: 403 Forbidden. 401 means not logged in at all.

options: An app running on your own computer
An app running on a shared test server
A website that is live for everyone
A page saved in your browser's cache
quiz.why: localhost = this computer. 5173 is the port.

quiz.q: Submitting a sign-up form usually sends which kind of request?
quiz.why: POST sends or creates data. GET fetches, PATCH updates something that exists.

quiz.q: Your API starts returning `429`. What does it mean?
quiz.why: 429 = rate limited. Common with AI APIs.
